topic: Day 2 · Metabolic Emergencies — Tumour Lysis, Refeeding & Rhabdomyolysis
speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Medicine & Critical Care
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Critical Care Unit
speakerBio: Intensivist with a nephrology bent who runs the hospital's electrolyte-emergency simulation course and teaches that the most dangerous derangements come not from failing organs but from cells spilling their contents.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 58-year-old man with newly diagnosed high-grade B-cell lymphoma gets his first dose of chemotherapy at 9am. By midnight the nurse calls: he is confused, twitching, and his monitor shows peaked T waves. The 3am bloods land like a grenade — K⁺ 6.9, phosphate 3.1 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.62, urate 780 µmol/L, creatinine tripled from baseline. Nothing was bleeding, nothing was infected. His own tumour, dissolving under the chemotherapy, has poured its intracellular contents into his blood and clogged his kidneys. This is a metabolic emergency — a derangement not of a failing organ but of cells spilling their contents. Today we cover the four that trip up the on-call doctor: tumour lysis, refeeding, rhabdomyolysis and the potassium trap of DKA. They share a single theme — what is inside cells is dangerous outside them, and the kidney is caught in the crossfire.

1 · 🧨 Tumour lysis syndrome — the tumour that kills after you treat it

Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is the massive, sudden release of intracellular contents when a large, rapidly-dividing, chemo-sensitive tumour is killed. Potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids (metabolised to urate) flood the circulation faster than the kidney can clear them. It is the price of a treatment working too well.

The four biochemical hits — and why each is dangerous

AbnormalityMechanismDanger
HyperkalaemiaK⁺ is the dominant intracellular cation, dumped on lysisThe earliest killer — fatal arrhythmia, often before other results are back
HyperphosphataemiaMalignant cells are phosphate-rich (up to 4× normal)Precipitates with calcium → acute nephrocalcinosis and AKI
HypocalcaemiaCalcium precipitates with the excess phosphate (calcium phosphate)Tetany, seizures, QT prolongation, arrhythmia
HyperuricaemiaPurine nucleic acids → xanthine → uric acidUric-acid crystals obstruct tubules → AKI; worse in acid urine

All four then converge on the kidney: uric-acid and calcium-phosphate crystals precipitate in the tubules, causing an obstructive/crystal-nephropathy AKI — which in turn destroys the kidney's ability to clear the very potassium and phosphate that are rising. A vicious cycle: the AKI worsens every other number.

TLS is the one oncological emergency where the treatment causes the crisis — anticipate it before the first dose, not after the arrhythmia.

Cairo–Bishop criteria — defining it precisely

Laboratory TLS = two or more of the following within 3 days before to 7 days after cytotoxic therapy: urate ≥476 µmol/L (8 mg/dL), K⁺ ≥6.0, phosphate ≥1.45 mmol/L (adults), or calcium ≤1.75 mmol/L — or a 25% change from baseline. Clinical TLS = laboratory TLS PLUS one of: AKI (creatinine rise), a cardiac arrhythmia/sudden death, or a seizure. The distinction matters: clinical TLS is the one with end-organ damage and drives escalation to dialysis.

⚠️ Who is at highest risk — flag them before chemo

High tumour burden + high proliferation + high chemosensitivity = danger: Burkitt lymphoma, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high-grade lymphomas, AML with high white count, bulky disease, high baseline LDH/urate, and — critically — pre-existing renal impairment or volume depletion. TLS can even occur spontaneously in very high-turnover tumours before any treatment. Every one of these patients needs a risk assessment and prophylaxis documented before cycle one.

2 · 🚰 Preventing and treating TLS — hydration, rasburicase, and when to dialyse

Prevention is the whole game

  • Aggressive IV hydration — the cornerstone. 2.5–3 L/m²/day of crystalloid, started 24–48h before therapy, to maintain a high urine output (target ~100 mL/m²/h) and flush crystals through the tubules before they precipitate. Volume dilutes every offending solute and preserves renal perfusion.
  • Urate-lowering — match the drug to the risk:
AllopurinolRasburicase
MechanismXanthine oxidase inhibitor — blocks new urate formationRecombinant urate oxidase — enzymatically destroys existing urate → soluble allantoin
Effect on existing urateNone — only prevents moreRapid, dramatic fall within hours
DownsideCan accumulate xanthine (its own crystal nephropathy); slowCost; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (causes haemolysis); breaks down urate in the sample tube (draw on ice)
UseLow/intermediate risk, prophylaxisHigh risk or established hyperuricaemia/TLS
💡 Allopurinol PREVENTS, rasburicase DESTROYS

Allopurinol stops the tap; it does nothing to the urate already in the bath. Rasburicase pulls the plug — it enzymatically converts existing uric acid to soluble allantoin and drops the level within hours. So high-risk or established TLS gets rasburicase; low-risk prophylaxis gets allopurinol. Never rely on allopurinol to rescue an established hyperuricaemic AKI. And check G6PD first — rasburicase triggers haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficiency.

🎯 The urine-alkalinisation reversal

Older protocols alkalinised the urine to make urate more soluble. This is now discouraged: raising urine pH makes uric acid more soluble but makes calcium phosphate LESS soluble, trading urate nephropathy for calcium-phosphate nephropathy — a bad swap in a hyperphosphataemic patient. With rasburicase available, plain aggressive hydration is preferred. Mechanism beats dogma.

Treating established derangements & when to dialyse

  • Hyperkalaemia — treat as the emergency it is (calcium gluconate to protect the myocardium, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol to shift; see the DKA section for the shift logic). This is the number that kills first.
  • Hyperphosphataemia — phosphate binders, hydration; do NOT give calcium unless symptomatic hypocalcaemia (adding calcium to high phosphate worsens precipitation).
  • Hypocalcaemia — treat only if symptomatic (tetany, seizures, arrhythmia) — replacing calcium into a high-phosphate milieu drives calcium-phosphate deposition in tissues and kidney.
⚠️ Indications for urgent dialysis in TLS

Escalate to renal replacement therapy (KDIGO indications, plus TLS-specific severity) when there is: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe hyperphosphataemia with symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload / oliguric AKI unresponsive to therapy, or uraemia. TLS often needs early, aggressive dialysis (high phosphate clearance) — involve nephrology before the biochemistry becomes unmanageable, not as a last rite.

3 · 🍽️ Refeeding syndrome — the danger of feeding the starved

Refeeding syndrome is the potentially lethal shift in fluids and electrolytes when a chronically starved patient is fed — orally, enterally or parenterally. It is iatrogenic, entirely preventable, and still kills, because the intervention that saves the patient (nutrition) is the trigger.

The mechanism — an insulin surge with empty stores

In starvation the body switches to fat and protein for fuel; insulin falls, and intracellular phosphate, potassium and magnesium are depleted even though serum levels may look normal (the body cannibalises stores to keep serum steady). Then you feed carbohydrate:

  1. A carbohydrate load triggers a surge of insulin.
  2. Insulin drives glucose, phosphate, potassium and magnesium INTO cells — and switches on anabolism, which consumes yet more phosphate to build ATP and phosphorylated intermediates.
  3. Serum phosphate, potassium and magnesium plummet — profound hypophosphataemia is the hallmark.
  4. Meanwhile carbohydrate metabolism burns through thiamine (a cofactor), unmasking deficiency → Wernicke's encephalopathy.
  5. Insulin's antinatriuretic effect causes sodium and fluid retention → oedema and cardiac overload in a heart wasted by starvation.
Refeeding hypophosphataemia is insulin sweeping phosphate into cells that have no reserves to spare — feed slowly, replace first, and give thiamine before the first calorie.

Who is at risk — the NICE criteria

🎯 NICE high-risk criteria for refeeding

One or more of: BMI <16, unintentional weight loss >15% in 3–6 months, little/no intake >10 days, or low baseline K⁺/phosphate/Mg before feeding. OR two or more of: BMI <18.5, weight loss >10%, little/no intake >5 days, or a history of alcohol misuse or drugs including insulin, chemotherapy, antacids or diuretics. Think of it in the anorexia nervosa patient, the chronic alcoholic, the post-bariatric or malabsorptive patient, the neglected elderly admission, and the prolonged NBM inpatient.

Managing it — thiamine first, calories cautiously, replace relentlessly

  • Thiamine BEFORE feeding — 200–300 mg (IV Pabrinex in the high-risk/alcoholic) started before or with the first calories, continued daily; plus a vitamin B-complex and multivitamin. Never give a carbohydrate load to a thiamine-deplete patient first — you can precipitate Wernicke's.
  • Start low, go slow — begin at 10 kcal/kg/day (as low as 5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, e.g. BMI <14 or negligible intake >15 days), building to full needs over 4–7 days.
  • Replace electrolytes proactively — correct/replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium during feeding; do NOT wait for feeding to correct them and do NOT necessarily delay feeding for mild derangement — replace alongside.
  • Monitor — daily (initially twice-daily) phosphate, potassium, magnesium, glucose; fluid balance and clinical signs of overload.
ElectrolyteWhy it fallsConsequence if ignored
PhosphateInsulin-driven cellular uptake + ATP synthesisCardiac & respiratory muscle failure, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, death — the signature lesion
PotassiumInsulin shifts K⁺ intracellularlyArrhythmia
MagnesiumCellular uptake; depleted storesArrhythmia; refractory hypokalaemia/hypocalcaemia until Mg replaced
ThiamineConsumed as a cofactor for carbohydrate metabolismWernicke's encephalopathy / wet beriberi (heart failure)

4 · 💪 Rhabdomyolysis — the electrolyte storm from dying muscle

When skeletal muscle breaks down (crush injury, prolonged immobility/long lie, seizures, statins, exertion, ischaemia, sepsis), it spills its contents: myoglobin, creatine kinase, and — like every cell — potassium and phosphate. The result is a stereotyped electrolyte storm plus a myoglobin-driven AKI.

The sequence of derangements

  • Hyperkalaemia — potassium poured from necrotic muscle; can be extreme and rapid, the early killer, worsened by any concurrent AKI.
  • Hyperphosphataemia — phosphate released from muscle.
  • EARLY hypocalcaemia — calcium precipitates with the released phosphate into damaged muscle, and there is skeletal resistance to PTH. Do not treat it unless symptomatic — the calcium is sequestered, not lost.
  • LATE rebound HYPERcalcaemia — during recovery, the calcium that deposited in muscle is mobilised back out, and PTH/vitamin-D activity rebounds → the same patient who was hypocalcaemic on day 2 becomes hypercalcaemic on day 7. This is why you must not aggressively replace calcium early — you set up a dangerous rebound.
  • Hyperuricaemia — purine release adds to the crystal load on the kidney.
  • Myoglobinuric AKI — myoglobin is directly tubulotoxic, causes tubular obstruction (casts), and vasoconstriction; worse in acidic, volume-deplete urine.
Rhabdo calcium is a moving target: LOW early (trapped in muscle), HIGH late (released back). Treat early hypocalcaemia only if symptomatic, or you will overshoot into the rebound.

Treatment — fluids, fluids, fluids

  • Aggressive IV crystalloid is the mainstay — early and generous (often several litres, titrated to a urine output of ~200–300 mL/h) to maintain renal perfusion and flush myoglobin through before it precipitates. Started early, it can prevent the AKI entirely.
  • Isotonic saline is the standard fluid. Bicarbonate/mannitol have not been shown superior to adequate saline volume and are not routinely recommended — the evidence favours simple, early, high-volume crystalloid.
  • Treat hyperkalaemia urgently and monitor phosphate/calcium; dialyse for the usual refractory indications (hyperkalaemia, overload, uraemia, severe AKI).
  • Watch for compartment syndrome — aggressive fluids can worsen limb compartment pressures; it is a surgical emergency.
⚠️ The calcium trap in rhabdomyolysis

A twitchy, hypocalcaemic rhabdo patient invites the reflex to give calcium. Resist it unless there is symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizure, arrhythmia, or severe hyperkalaemia needing cardiac membrane stabilisation). The early calcium is not lost — it is deposited in injured muscle and will be released back during recovery, causing rebound hypercalcaemia. Over-replace early and you convert a self-limiting hypocalcaemia into a symptomatic hypercalcaemia a week later.

5 · 🩸 DKA electrolyte handling — the potassium paradox

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the emergency where the potassium number lies most dangerously — and the rules exist precisely to stop you killing the patient with insulin. The key is to separate serum potassium from total-body potassium.

Why the serum K⁺ is high but total-body K⁺ is catastrophically low

  1. Insulin deficiency and acidaemia both drive potassium OUT of cells into the serum (H⁺ enters cells in exchange for K⁺; without insulin, K⁺ cannot be held intracellularly).
  2. The osmotic diuresis of hyperglycaemia then pours that potassium out in the urine, along with vomiting losses — so the whole-body potassium store is being depleted, often by hundreds of mmol.
  3. Net result: a patient who is total-body potassium DEPLETED presents with a serum K⁺ that is normal or even HIGH. The high serum number hides an empty tank.
🎯 What insulin does to that hidden deficit

When you give insulin (and fluids, and correct the acidosis), potassium is driven rapidly back into cells. The serum K⁺ falls fast. In a patient whose total-body potassium is already empty, this unmasks a life-threatening hypokalaemia within hours — precipitating fatal arrhythmia. This is why insulin is never the first move if the potassium is low.

The potassium rule — memorise it exactly

Serum K⁺ at presentationAction
> 5.5 mmol/L (or unknown/anuric)Start insulin; give NO potassium yet; recheck K⁺ frequently
3.5 – 5.5 mmol/LStart insulin AND add potassium to the fluids (typically 40 mmol/L)
< 3.5 mmol/LDo NOT start insulin. Replace potassium first (often needs a monitored/critical-care setting) until K⁺ > 3.5, THEN start insulin
In DKA the serum potassium is a liar. Check it, replace it, and NEVER start insulin if K⁺ < 3.5 — you will drive the last of it into cells and stop the heart.

6 · 🗂️ Master tables — the electrolyte fingerprints side by side

SyndromeK⁺PhosphateCalciumUrateKidneyCornerstone Rx
Tumour lysisHighHighLowHighCrystal AKIHydration + rasburicase/allopurinol; dialysis
RefeedingLowVery lowLow (with low Mg)—Usually sparedThiamine first; 10 kcal/kg; replace PO₄/K/Mg
RhabdomyolysisHighHighLow early → High lateHighMyoglobin AKIAggressive saline; treat K⁺; don't over-give Ca early
DKA (at presentation)High serum / low total bodyLow (falls with insulin)——Pre-renal / osmoticFluids + insulin + K⁺ rule; never insulin if K <3.5
💡 The unifying one-liner

Three of these four (TLS, rhabdo, DKA-at-presentation) are cells dumping their contents OUT → high serum K⁺ and phosphate. Refeeding, and DKA-once-you-treat-it, are insulin driving everything back IN → low phosphate and potassium. Know which direction the electrolytes are moving and the management writes itself: block the release and protect the kidney, or replace before you shift.

☠️ M&M — the anorexia patient fed to death

A 22-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa (BMI 12, negligible intake for three weeks) was admitted and, with good intentions, started on a full 2000 kcal enteral feed on day one to 'build her up quickly.' No thiamine was given first, and electrolytes were checked only once daily. By the second morning her phosphate was 0.28 mmol/L and magnesium 0.4; overnight she developed heart failure and a fatal ventricular arrhythmia. What went wrong: a textbook refeeding syndrome — a full calorie load into an empty, insulin-primed body swept phosphate and potassium into cells, thiamine was never replaced, and monitoring was too infrequent to catch the crash. Lessons: in a high-risk patient start at 5–10 kcal/kg/day, give thiamine (Pabrinex) before the first calorie, replace phosphate/potassium/magnesium proactively, and check electrolytes at least daily (twice daily in the first days). The feed that was meant to save her killed her because it was given too fast. Slower would have been safer.

7 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Tumour lysis = cells spilling out: high K⁺, high phosphate, low calcium, high urate → crystal AKI. Cairo–Bishop defines it (lab vs clinical). Prevent with aggressive hydration; allopurinol prevents new urate while rasburicase destroys existing urate (check G6PD). Dialyse for refractory K⁺/phosphate/overload/uraemia.
  2. Refeeding = insulin sweeping electrolytes in: the hallmark is profound hypophosphataemia. Identify the high-risk patient (NICE), give thiamine before feeding, start at 10 kcal/kg/day, and replace phosphate/potassium/magnesium proactively.
  3. Rhabdomyolysis: high K⁺ and phosphate, early hypocalcaemia then late rebound HYPERcalcaemia — do NOT over-replace calcium early. The mainstay is early, aggressive isotonic fluids; bicarbonate/mannitol add nothing over adequate saline.
  4. DKA potassium paradox: serum K⁺ high but total-body depleted. Follow the rule — K >5.5 hold potassium; 3.5–5.5 replace with insulin; K <3.5 replace FIRST and do not start insulin.
  5. Know the direction of movement: out-of-cell syndromes (TLS, rhabdo, presenting DKA) → protect the kidney and treat hyperkalaemia; into-cell syndromes (refeeding, treated DKA) → replace before you shift.

moderatorQs.q: Why is rasburicase preferred over allopurinol in a high-risk patient about to start chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the two drugs act at completely different points. Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor — it only prevents formation of new uric acid and does nothing to the large urate load a high-turnover tumour like Burkitt will generate; it also works slowly and can cause xanthine accumulation. Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase that enzymatically converts existing uric acid to soluble allantoin, dropping the level within hours and dissolving the crystal load already threatening the kidney. In a high tumour-burden, high-LDH, high-urate patient you need to eliminate urate that is already there, so rasburicase is preferred — after checking G6PD status, since it precipitates haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficiency, and remembering to transport the sample on ice.

moderatorQs.q: A patient with BMI 13 and no intake for two weeks is admitted. The team wants to start full feeding today. What is your advice?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Stop — this is a textbook refeeding-syndrome setup. Full calories into a chronically starved, insulin-primed body will drive phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and can cause fatal hypophosphataemia, arrhythmia and cardiac failure within 24–48 hours. Instead: give thiamine (IV Pabrinex) before the first calorie to prevent Wernicke's, plus a B-complex/multivitamin; start feeding at only 5–10 kcal/kg/day and escalate over 4–7 days; check and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium proactively alongside feeding (do not wait for them to fall); and monitor these electrolytes and fluid balance at least daily, twice daily initially. Feeding is the treatment, but the speed of feeding is what kills.

moderatorQs.q: A rhabdomyolysis patient has a corrected calcium of 1.70 on day 2. Should you replace it, and what will happen later?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Only if she is symptomatic — tetany, seizures, an arrhythmia, or as membrane stabilisation for dangerous hyperkalaemia. The early hypocalcaemia of rhabdomyolysis is not true depletion: calcium has precipitated with released phosphate into the damaged muscle, with added skeletal PTH resistance. It is sequestered, not lost. During recovery that calcium is mobilised back into the circulation, and with rebounding PTH/vitamin-D activity the patient characteristically swings into hypercalcaemia around day 5–7. So aggressively replacing calcium early sets up a symptomatic rebound hypercalcaemia later. Treat the hypocalcaemia only when it is causing harm, and warn the team to watch the calcium climb during recovery.

audienceQs.q: In DKA, the potassium is 5.9 and the patient looks unwell — surely I should just start the insulin straight away?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Start the insulin, yes, but do not add potassium to the fluids yet because the serum K⁺ is above 5.5 — recheck it frequently. The crucial thing is that this serum number is misleadingly high: the patient's total-body potassium is severely depleted (driven out of cells by acidosis and insulin lack, then lost in the osmotic diuresis and vomiting). As soon as insulin and fluids take effect, potassium pours back into cells and the serum level falls fast. So follow the rule: K >5.5 → insulin, no added K⁺; K 3.5–5.5 → insulin plus 40 mmol/L K⁺; K <3.5 → replace potassium FIRST and hold the insulin until it is above 3.5, or you can precipitate a fatal hypokalaemic arrhythmia.

audienceQs.q: For our tumour-lysis prophylaxis protocol, what do I need to check before dispensing rasburicase?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Three things. First, G6PD status — rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide as it breaks down urate, causing severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD-deficient patients, so it is contraindicated there (use allopurinol instead). Second, a pregnancy check (it's contraindicated). Third, advise the lab that any uric acid sample must be drawn into a pre-chilled tube and kept on ice and analysed promptly, because rasburicase continues to degrade urate ex vivo and will give a falsely low result otherwise. Also confirm the patient is on aggressive IV hydration alongside — the drug lowers urate but hydration is what protects the kidney — and note that urine alkalinisation is no longer recommended.

audienceQs.q: When should I be calling for dialysis in tumour lysis rather than just medically managing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Escalate early — TLS often outruns medical therapy. The specific triggers are: refractory hyperkalaemia not controlled by shift/binding measures, severe hyperphosphataemia (especially with symptomatic hypocalcaemia, where you can't give calcium safely), oliguric AKI or fluid overload unresponsive to fluids, and uraemic complications — the standard KDIGO RRT indications, applied with a low threshold. Because the phosphate and potassium loads keep regenerating as more tumour lyses, continuous modalities (CVVHDF) give better sustained clearance. The key message is to involve nephrology before the biochemistry becomes unmanageable rather than waiting for an arrhythmia or a peri-arrest — anticipation, not rescue.
